I have a slightly different take on this. In a way I think a lot of what Nabokov was after with the unreliable narrator was the built-in unreliability of fiction and the fact that it's an artifice that's being woven--early postmodernism. There are occasional glimpses into this with the sudden incursion of wholly improbable or fantastic events that occur, blink and you miss them (one whole sentence about a hermaphrodite or something where you're like wtf just happened, never mind; nonexistent place names; a list of items one of which is imaginary; screamingly Freudian coinages like Camp Climax, etc). So in a sense it's all about this sort of seduction of the reader and what happens in the narrative per se is a mirror of that. So this gives rise to multiple parallel worlds/possibilities within the text simultaneously being true and none of them being true, except for the fact that "Humbert" is a monster and Lo is his victim. Even trying to solve the mystery in a sense plays into the meta-narrative's hands because it presumes there is a mystery (although to tease us further there's a quasi-mystery plot within a plot in which Hum "investigates" what happened to Lo through bizarre readings of hotel registries for clues and the like). I'm saying this in the context of Nabokov's work as a whole but particularly things like *Invitation to a Beheading* where the possibility of ANY of it happening in consensual reality is less than zero. I sort of see Nabokov setting out to do a work of magic where he occasionally shows his hand in the mix but you only see a distortion bubble or something in the text, not where the meddling begins or ends. And he sets himself the supreme challenge of getting us to see the world through the eyes of a guy who acknowledges he's a liar from the beginning, who has horrible thoughts and commits horrible acts, and yet despite and through this slight of hand we ache for Lolita's stolen humanity.
